description: We're team roamer, building AstroLens for NASA Space Apps: point your phone at the night sky to name stars, and use our Earth Analogs engine to find where on Earth we should test Moon/Mars hardware. 34 sites scored on one 500 m grid — Chhusang currently leads, with Kagbeni (the 2019 NASA MAU-Nepal site) close behind. App, APK and 29 s demo live now (sushant-me.github.io/roamer).
summary: AstroLens (team roamer) is a space learning app with seven features. Our NASA Space Apps challenge asks for Earth locations that analog Moon and Mars base sites: the Earth Analogs feature scores 34 sites on one 500 m grid, shows where the analogy breaks, and ranks them by Survey Gap — where a field survey pays off. Two controls anchor it: Atacama passes every check but scores 0.00 because it is already studied; Pokhara fails aridity and scores 0.00. Chhusang leads (gap 0.23). The rest makes it a real learning tool: AR sky camera, gyro sky dome, 3D solar system, Tonight's Sky, 88 constellations, and Story of Earth. NASA data, traceable numbers, limits stated in-app.
details:
AstroLens is a space learning app by team roamer for NASA Space Apps 2026 (Bhaktapur, Virtual). Seven features; the submitted challenge answer is the Earth Analogs engine.

Challenge answer: 34 characterized records on one 500 m grid, a quantified mismatch ledger, and a Survey Gap ranking = similarity × (1 − literature attention) × operability. It is a shortlist for investigation, not a certification. Positive control Atacama passes 5/5 but scores gap 0.00 because it is already studied; negative control Pokhara fails aridity and scores 0.00; Chhusang leads (0.23, range 0.23–0.31 under two literature proxies), Kagbeni second (0.16). Weights ±20% keep the top unchanged 10/10; thresholds ±20% move 16 labels but not the ranking.

Where the data comes from: 34 records = 33 Nepal test-range sites + Atacama control (Chile); coordinates/altitude sampled from the DEM, operability is an analyst score 0–1 with access notes. Terrain: AWS Terrain Tiles (Terrarium, SRTM-derived), z12 native ~30–34 m block-averaged to 500 m; variables: elevation, local relief (1.5 km), landscape relief (12 km), median/IQR slope, roughness, variogram slope. Climate: Open-Meteo Archive API (ERA5, 2015–2024, 0.25° ≈ 28 km); precipitation, seasonal and diurnal air-temperature amplitude, shortwave radiation. Context only: NASA POWER MERRA-2 skin temperature (0.5° × 0.625°) and ERA5-Land soil 6 cm (0.1° ≈ 9 km). Attention: OpenAlex keyword count, normalized log10(count+1)/4, with a Crossref proxy check (r ≈ 0.69). Targets: NASA PDS MOLA and THEMIS/Diviner summaries → relief 800 ± 400 m, slope 4 ± 3°, seasonal amplitude 45 ± 12 K, noon elevation 40 ± 12°. Weights: similarity = 0.45 terrain + 0.15 thermal + 0.15 illumination + 0.25 aridity; each dimension is |x − target| in target-σ units scored 1/(1+d). Gates: slope ≤10°, relief 20–1,500 m, noon Sun ≥20°, precipitation <800 mm/yr, operability ≥0.5; gap = similarity × (1 − attention) × operability. All of this is in the app's METHOD tab.

Why it matters: NASA tests instruments, procedures and science operations at Earth analog sites before risking them on the Moon or Mars; a transparent shortlist of where a field campaign adds the most new information is a small but real planning tool.

Validation and zero scores: Atacama (studied) and Pokhara (fails aridity) both score 0.00 by design; 0.00 means already well-surveyed or gated out, not a failed computation, and the UI says so. Known analogs screen as heavily studied (proxy gap ≈0.00; Askja 0.07); Chhusang/Kagbeni sit where similarity is high and attention is low. Ranking is robust to weight changes; threshold changes move labels, not order.

Scope and focus: Sky Camera, AR Explorer, Tonight's Sky and Learn the Sky share one HYG catalogue — AR Explorer and Sky Dome are modes inside Sky Camera — so the seven tiles are one product. 3D Solar System and Story of Earth are engagement. If forced to cut one: 3D Solar System; the challenge answer stays.

Sensors, offline, drift: AR pointing fuses accelerometer and magnetometer with low-pass smoothing; compass drift near metal/magnets is real, so the app offers manual aim, GYRO ON/OFF and RESET VIEW instead of claiming absolute accuracy. GPS comes from geolocator; if denied/unavailable the app falls back to Kathmandu and says so. Star, constellation and image data are bundled, so sky features work offline; only optional NASA lookups need a connection.

Accuracy checks: 267-star catalogue cross-checked against HYG v4.1 by HIP identifier (RA, Dec, magnitude); all 88 IAU constellations with brightest-star fields checked against HYG membership; demo alt/az independently recomputed with a standard sidereal-time formula; two controls plus sensitivity runs guard the ranking.

Other features: Sky Camera names nearest bright stars with manual fallback; Sky Dome is gyro- or drag-driven; Tonight's Sky lists what is above you; Learn the Sky covers 267 stars and 88 constellations; 3D Solar System has all eight planets with real NASA images, galaxies and a Beyond tab (Kuiper Belt, heliopause, Oort Cloud, Voyager 1, observable universe — schematic, not to scale, as the app says); Story of Earth scrubs 4.57 Gyr to today across 11 stages with materials, composition, a playable film and five hypotheses each with evidence and its open problem.

Honest limits: regional shortlist (Nepal + Atacama), not a global survey; SRTM elevation only, no geology/regolith; ERA5/MERRA-2 too coarse for mountain microclimates (500 m vs ~9/50 km); no MODIS skin temperature; operability is an analyst judgment; star pointing is low-precision and sensor-dependent with manual fallback — a learning tool, not a planetarium-grade ephemeris. The 29-second demo narration is SI-generated (text-to-speech) and disclosed as required.

Review and tools: methodological feedback from Arun Lohar (@arunlohar11) on Space Apps Connect was incorporated (threshold/proxy sensitivity, suitability vs research priority, resolution and data limits). Tools: Flutter/Dart (web + Android), GitHub Pages, GitHub Releases, Node/Python pipeline, AWS Terrarium, Open-Meteo, NASA POWER, OpenAlex, NASA PDS, HYG.
